lines: Take {gift_item}. Good gear should travel, not gather dust.
Here, {gift_item}. It has more use with you than sitting by my cauldron.
Good. {gift_item} sat well with {tested_villager}, like softened leather.
Then the fit was comfortable. {tested_villager} liked {gift_item}.
Too stiff for them, then. For {gift_subject}, try {alternative_gift}.
{gift_item} rubbed wrong? Bring {alternative_gift}; better fit, less complaint.

messages.text: That advice chafed. {alternative_gift} should sit easier.
You wore bad advice too long. Trade it for {alternative_gift}.

openings.text: Mind the tannery. What do you need?

closings.text: Back to curing leather without wasting hide, then.

pacify.text: Fine. I will stitch this shut for now.
That is not enough to mend it. Bring {emerald_cost} {emeralds}.
No. This split runs too deep for {payment_items}.

lines: Bad stitching in the rain tells on itself quickly.
Gear that lasts is mostly patience made visible.
A stitch done poorly waits for the worst time to confess.
Good leather is patience you can wear.
Rain tells the truth about gear faster than any seller will.
A pack should carry weight without reminding you every step.
A split seam can ruin a journey faster than a bad map.
I once made boots that outlasted three owners and four bad roads.
My apron has seen enough mistakes to deserve its own corner by the fire.

lines.text: Mind the tannery. The smell is honest, at least.
Leather jokes need a thick skin. I keep saying that until someone laughs.
That sentence split like cheap stitching.
Do not mock work that lasts longer than your manners.

lines: I remember being stitched back into myself. Your hands held the thread.
The cure left scars, but good leather can carry scars. So can I.
Your face is worn into the memory, but the edges are rough.
I remember straps, shaking, and a second chance pulled tight.

lines.text: I remember you, and I remember the tearing. Both are true.

lines: Thunder shook the cauldron so hard the cauldron shook rings across the water, but everyone near me is still standing.
I checked hides, saddles, and dye vats after the lightning, then counted heads. No one should be alone after a sky like that.
Near the cauldron, the bell sounded small under that thunder. We stayed inside and kept the doors watched.
That thunder made everyone quiet. I checked the hides twice.
The sky can keep its lightning. I have hides to set right.
I checked dry hides and dye racks for sparks first, then checked faces for smoke and fear.
We passed water hand to hand and kept people away from the smoke. I checked the cauldron after.
The hides can wait. People come first.
We saved what we could reach around the cauldron, then stopped pretending things matter more than neighbors.
The smoke is thinning near the cauldron, but everyone is still sniffing the air like it might lie.
During a raid, the hides can soak another day; who makes it behind a door matters more.
The horns stopped, but my hands near the cauldron still expect another wave from the road.
We counted living neighbors before hides, saddles, and dye vats. That is the only count worth starting with.
Raiders came looking for easy emeralds. They found barred doors near the cauldron and a bell that would not stop ringing.
From the cauldron, I saw fear cross the square; then I saw courage get there first.
Night trouble tests the loose latch by the cauldron first. We are fixing those before sunset.
I stayed near the cauldron corner and listened for anyone calling from the dark.
Dawn gave the cauldron enough light to count wounds, missing blocks, and who made it home.
The dark tested everyone. Most of us passed by keeping stout boots between us and teeth.
We are safe enough near the cauldron, though every shadow is being inspected twice.
The wind threw sand through every crack. I am still cleaning sand out of the leather seams.
I checked hides, saddles, and dye vats, then checked who was coughing too hard to answer.
Sand reached the cauldron, the hinges, and half our eyes, but no one has been reported missing.
A hard wind teaches a leatherworker which doors actually close and which ones only pretend.
We are safe enough near the cauldron, though the whole village sounds like it is chewing gravel.
The hides can soak another day. Warm hands, clear paths, and full hearths come first.
Snow piled against the doors, but everyone near the cauldron found shelter.
Cold works quietly around the cauldron. We are checking on anyone who stayed quiet too long.
I am clearing stiff frost from the hides and watching for footprints that stop too soon.
We are alright for now near the cauldron. Keep the fires fed and the paths open.
